title: Amazon and Google will together own nearly 30% of Anthropic after its IPO
content:
Anthropic on Tuesday disclosed more details about the biggest investment agreements with major cloud providers Amazon and Google.
While we already knew that Amazon stood to make a killing on its Anthropic investments from the IPO, Anthropic revealed that Amazon’s total stake will come in at just shy of 15% (14.7% to be exact).
Even more interesting is that Amazon could have, if it wished, owned an even bigger share of the company. When Amazon invested billions in Anthropic in 2023 and 2024 (long before Claude Code took the enterprise world by storm, back in the days when Anthropic looked like it would forever be a speck in OpenAI’s shadow), the cloud giant obtained promissory notes that could convert into equity.
These notes carry conversion prices of about $2.09 or $5.05 per share, depending on the year of investment. Amazon has opted to convert a chunk of them as part of the IPO into a special class of non-voting shares that will give it about 15% ownership. (The shares can receive dividends and convert to standard voting Class A shares when sold, the filing says).
But it has also opted to hold on to billions of dollars’ worth of the notes for now. If it converted them all right now, it would own just under 24% of Anthropic (23.8% to be precise).
Google, meanwhile, will own just under 14% (13.7%), also in non-voting shares, which come from the conversion of notes, as well as the “private placement” sale of shares as part of this IPO. A group of major tech companies (AMD, Broadcom, Google, Micron, Microsoft, Nvidia, and TSMC Partners) have agreed to buy $26 billion worth of this non-voting stock. Google and Nvidia each agreed to buy $10 billion worth.
So while a lot of investors stand to make billions of dollars in Anthropic’s IPO, Amazon is one of the biggest winners, and that doesn’t even count that AWS stands to earn from Anthropic’s commitment to spend more than $100 billion on its cloud services over the next decade.

report.summary: Anthropic's IPO filing shows Amazon will hold 14.7% and Google 13.7% in non-voting shares, with Amazon holding notes that could lift its stake to 23.8%.
report.background: Anthropic was founded in 2021 by former OpenAI researchers and built its business on Claude models. Because frontier training requires enormous compute, it raised money from the same cloud providers it buys capacity from: Amazon committed roughly $8 billion across 2023 and 2024, and Google also invested, in both cases largely through convertible notes rather than straight equity. That structure let the hyperscalers wait and see while Anthropic was still a distant second to OpenAI, before Claude Code turned enterprise coding into a fast-growing revenue line. Anthropic's listing is among the largest AI IPOs to date, and it lands in an era when model labs and cloud providers are increasingly entangled through equity stakes, compute commitments and joint customers. The filing also details a $26 billion private placement of non-voting stock that lets chipmakers and rivals buy in.
key_points: Combined, Amazon and Google will control just under 30% of Anthropic after the IPO: 14.7% for Amazon and 13.7% for Google. Both packages consist of non-voting shares, which can receive dividends and convert into standard voting Class A stock when sold.

Amazon deliberately left money on the table. It converted only part of its promissory notes, which carry conversion prices of about $2.09 or $5.05 per share. If Amazon converted everything today, it would hold about 23.8% of Anthropic, keeping significant upside in reserve.

A group of chip and cloud giants, including AMD, Broadcom, Google, Micron, Microsoft, Nvidia and TSMC Partners, agreed to buy $26 billion of non-voting stock in the IPO private placement. Google and Nvidia each committed $10 billion of that total.

The equity stake is only part of the return for AWS. Anthropic has committed to spend more than $100 billion on cloud services over the next decade, so Amazon profits from Anthropic both as an investor and as its largest compute supplier.

By using non-voting shares, Anthropic's leadership keeps control of the company while strategic backers capture financial upside. That structure handles governance questions that would otherwise dominate a public listing.
report.impact: For the AI industry, the IPO makes the ties between cloud providers and model labs explicit. Amazon and Google are simultaneously Anthropic's biggest shareholders, its landlords and its competitors through their own models, which creates circular-financing structures that regulators and public investors are likely to scrutinise. For developers, the stakes reinforce a two-cloud reality: Claude will remain cheapest and deepest on AWS Bedrock and Google Vertex AI, and pricing, rate limits and feature timing may follow commercial rather than purely technical logic. For regular users, the practical effect is that frontier AI is now exposed to public-market pressure through Anthropic's share price, making quarterly revenue expectations part of how models get funded and shipped. The IPO also gives ordinary investors their first direct way to own a pure-play frontier lab.
report.tools: To follow the story, watch Claude and Claude Code for product direction, AWS Bedrock and Google Cloud Vertex AI for deployment and pricing, and Anthropic's open-source Model Context Protocol for integration patterns. Track SEC S-1 and subsequent filings for stake conversions, and benchmark against open-weight rivals like Llama, Mistral and Qwen to judge how lock-in affects cost.
